companies.accountWall: Men (Hims): after 21 anonymous screens, at https://app.forhims.co.uk/start/signup?t=hair&anon_flow_key=hair — 'Ready to see if you’re eligible? Next we'll cover your health and medical history as well as treatment options.' asks for an email address. Women (Hers): at the first screen (first and last name).
companies.coverageNote: Stage 1 (map) walked the whole anonymous men's quiz and read the served quiz definition, product and price tables, app code and public documents. Stage 2 (experiment) replayed the baseline twice and then changed one answer at a time: 31 runs covering every non-baseline option of all 11 anonymous questions, so all 42 options have now been clicked live. Seven further runs checked two multi-select combinations, the phone layout, a returning visitor, skipping the quiz, two other landing pages and the Hers entry: 40 replays in all. Every run kept the full server traffic, which showed the server choosing the next step after each answer and returning no result at the end. Stage 2 also read ten more of the app's code files (how the server's eligibility result is used, the consent screen, brand settings) and the older Hims UK help centre (vitamin strengths in the chews). Not obtained, and not obtainable without an account: the wording of the medical questions, the rules that map answers to products, any live recommendation, and the checkout prices. Nothing at all could be tested on Hers UK, which asks for a name first. Stage 3 (verify) added 25 reviewer replays in runs/verify-* (two baselines, a full-trace baseline, six repeated one-change runs, and 16 runs on behaviour stage 2 had not tested or had tested once), re-read 16 public pages, re-read the served code behind every code-based rule, and re-read the leaflet and help-centre lines behind every document-based rule. The wall is where stage 1 and stage 2 said it is, and nothing behind it could be tested.
companies.engineSummary: Hims UK's engine has two parts, and only the first can be watched from outside. Part one is a marketing quiz anyone can take: 11 questions (intent, where, how much, when, goals, hair type, hair length, family history, stress, styling, time) with 10 selling screens between them. Stage 2 changed every answer one at a time (31 replays covering all 42 options) and the engine did not move: same screens, same order, same 'Great news—we have options that may work for you', same email wall. Six answers are repeated on one summary screen; the other five are never shown again. No answer stops anyone, warns anyone, or shows a product, strength or price. The server traffic agrees: after each answer the server names the next step, and at the end it returns a record id and nothing else. If the visitor signs up, his stored answers are attached to the new account. Part two sits behind the account: date of birth, a medical questionnaire, then a server-side rules step that marks each of ten products eligible or not and names one as the recommendation. A patient the server calls 'not eligible' sees a rejection screen. Everyone else sees one recommended product, with the other nine a tap away and the ruled-out ones greyed out as 'Not available based on your medical history'. The 'Selected based on your goals' chips on each product page are fixed text, not built from his answers. He then picks a plan length, ticks a consent box, gives GP details and pays up front; a clinician reviews the answers without a call and approves or refunds. The wording of the medical questions and the answer-to-product rules are not public. The best guides to them are Hims's own leaflets (who must not use each product) and the old platform's tag system, in which an answer could exclude every product tagged 'finasteride', 'minoxidil-oral', 'topical' and so on. Hers UK runs on the same platform with five minoxidil-based treatments for women, but asks for a name on the first screen, so nothing there can be tested without an account. Stage 3 (independent check): the reviewer replayed the baseline from fresh browsers and got the recorded end state, repeated six one-change runs with the same result, and tried what stage 2 had not: contradictory answers, every warning-sign answer together, going back, leaving and returning, deleting answers, a product code followed to the wall. None of it moves the engine before the wall. Everything said about the engine after the wall is still read from code, leaflets and help pages, or reasoned, and none of it was seen happening.
companies.verdict: The part of this report that can be watched from outside is solid. The anonymous Hims quiz was mapped completely, every option was tested by stage 2, and an independent reviewer got the same result from fresh browsers: 11 questions, one fixed path, no stop, no warning, no product, no price, then an email wall; Hers has no anonymous step at all. Those findings carry the label 'observed' and each one names its run folder. The product catalogue is also reliable for names, forms and strengths (checked on live pages and in the app's served files), and reasonably reliable for prices, with the caveat that most Hims prices come from one embedded price table of the old shop. The part a competitor most wants, how medical answers decide which product is offered, could not be observed within the research rules. What the report says about it is honestly labelled: the mechanics (the server marks each product eligible or not, names one as the recommendation, greys out the rest, or rejects outright) are read from served code and are trustworthy as a description of the code; the content of the rules (which answer removes which product) rests on leaflets, help pages and reasoning, and should be treated as informed expectation, not fact. Read with those labels in mind, the report can be trusted. It is rated 'partial' only because the engine behind the wall remains unseen.
topOpportunities: Give a real answer before asking for contact details: likely pattern, which treatments fit, which are ruled out and why, and the price. Hims asks 11 questions and returns nothing

Make the quiz respond. Not one of Hims's 42 options changes anything on screen. React at once: sudden or patchy loss → 'see a GP first'; shaved head or a hat every day → suggest tablets; heavy stress with no family history → explain shedding and offer a blood test
Ask the safety questions early (blood pressure, heart, mood, fertility plans, current medicines) and say in plain words when and why a product is ruled out, instead of a greyed-out card after sign-up

companies.engineSummary: Voy's real quiz could not be opened in any of the three stages, so this is the engine only as far as public evidence shows it. What was seen: (1) A pattern gate before the quiz. The men's and women's landing pages open a one-question pop-up. Its own script refuses 'Patchy' and 'Complete' (men) and 'Patchy hair loss' (women) with 'You aren't eligible', and sends everyone else to the quiz with a discount code attached. The verdict only appears after an email is given; ticking a refused option looks exactly like ticking an accepted one. The page aimed at both sexes shows the men's picture question to everyone. A separate pattern picker is pure marketing: every pattern leads to the same quiz link. (2) On an older Manual page that is still online, choosing 'Spray' instead of 'Tablets' switches the product (minoxidil capsules to 10% spray) at the same price, and choosing 3 months instead of 6 changes only the price and pack size. What was read in code, not seen running: an 11-month-old copy of the same web app (Manual, December 2025). There the quiz starts with a list of products, and each question can carry a reject list (one matching answer leaves no product and shows 'You aren't eligible', with a 'Review your answers' button), an exclude list (the answer removes named products and the quiz carries on) and parent or JSON Logic conditions (the answer opens, hides or rewords later questions). In that function an answer can only remove products, never add one. Which answers sit on which list is in a definition the app downloads at run time; it could not be read, and that code has no women's hair flow in it. What Voy publishes: lists of who should not have which medicine. DHT blockers (finasteride, dutasteride) are 'not suitable' for men trying for a baby or with a pregnant partner, men treated for an enlarged prostate, men who have had breast or prostate cancer, and men with severe depression; minoxidil 'should not be used' with low or uncontrolled blood pressure or a sore scalp, or over 65; under-18s, women (in the men's service) and men who are completely bald or do not have pattern hair loss are not treated. Whether the quiz applies each of these by removing a product, by warning, or by leaving it to the clinician was not seen. After the quiz, older code and Voy's pages point to: a recommendation (Voy leads with finasteride plus minoxidil together for men; women are offered minoxidil only, as serum or tablets, at a strength the clinician sets), a format and plan-length choice, add-ons (shampoo, vitamins), then the account, a medical-history questionnaire, photos and payment details, and a prescriber's review that sees flagged and changed answers. Older terms say payment is taken only on approval.
companies.verdict: Trust this report for three things: (1) what Voy shows in public before the quiz (the pop-up gates and their rules, the pattern picker, landing prices and product names, the women's offer), which was replayed again in stage 3 with the same results; (2) how the older Manual app's engine worked in December 2025, which was read in the code twice; and (3) which exclusions Voy publishes. Do not read it as a map of Voy's consultation. No quiz screen was reached in any stage because of a security checkpoint that was deliberately not worked around, so there is no question list, no option-by-option rule and no observed recommendation for the real quiz. The rules that tie a medical answer to a product are published cautions or reasoning from them, now labelled as such, and several strengths and prices rest on search-engine summaries of pages that would not open. After the corrections above the labels are honest: 'observed' always has a run folder behind it, 'code' has been re-read in the file, 'docs' means 'Voy publishes this', and everything else is 'inferred' or 'unknown'.
topOpportunities: Give the verdict before asking for contact details, and never dead-end: for patchy, sudden or complete loss explain the likely causes and route to a clinician review, a GP letter or a dermatology referral.

Diagnose properly where Voy appears only to screen (its quiz could not be seen): ask about speed of loss, shedding, scalp symptoms, periods and menopause, recent illness, diet and medicines; use baseline photos reviewed by a clinician before the first prescription; offer ferritin, thyroid and hormone tests when the answers point that way.

Build a real women's pathway (cause work-up, topical and oral minoxidil at stated strengths, spironolactone and other anti-androgens where appropriate, menopause link, postpartum advice) instead of one medicine for every cause.

companies.accountWall: Step 'yd', 'Personalise your account' (legal first name, legal last name, preferred name), reached by pressing 'Continue to checkout' on the shopping bag. Everything before it works without an account: all medical questions, date of birth, the UK tick and the bag. companies.coverageNote: Stage 1 mapped both routes to the account wall. Stage 2 ran 47 replays: 2 baseline replays, 39 one-change experiments and 6 group tests of non-medical answers, each compared with a pool of baseline visits because the server varies screens at random. Covered one change at a time: first tile, age (17 years 11 months, 18, 85), pregnancy, three men's and three women's hair-loss pictures, recent onset, scalp infection and eczema, blood pressure (and its follow-up), eight further men's conditions, PCOS and heart disease for women, postpartum, facial hair, two medicine options (antidepressants; Other + free text), minoxidil allergy, finasteride allergy, previous finasteride, drops versus capsules on both routes, declining finasteride / dutasteride, pets, and a second goal. Covered in group tests: gender identity (six options), hair type, styling, lifestyle statements, the other hair-loss pictures and timings, skin tone, scalp condition, six-month wishes, washing, hiding hair loss, hard water, buying stage and 'what influenced you'. Everything after the legal-name screen (account, photos, payment, the prescriber's choice of formula, check-ins) was not tested and is described from public documents only. Stage 3 (verify): 21 more replays (2 baselines, 17 one-change, 2 medical group tests), all one at a time; the stop, blood-pressure, pregnancy, gender-identity, pets, previous-product and promo rules were re-tested live (two goals, no hair loss and the 'Other' free-text boxes were not), and the 16 formulas and the price were re-checked against the live leaflets.
companies.engineSummary: Hair + Me's public consultation collects answers; it does not decide anything a visitor can see. Stage 2 replayed it 47 times (2 baseline replays, 39 experiments that changed one answer, and 6 group tests of non-medical answers) and compared every screen and the bag with a pool of baseline visits. Only a handful of answers do anything visible: sex at birth swaps the men's and women's question blocks; an age under 18 is the single hard stop; two or more goals, a blood-pressure diagnosis and 'pregnant, breastfeeding or likely to conceive' each add one screen; 'no hair loss' skips one; pets add a warning and a 'Better for pet owners' badge on The Capsules; previous treatments and 'Other' reveal a tick-box or a text box; and a gender identity other than man removes one marketing screen from the men's route. Everything else, including patchy or sudden loss, an active scalp infection, heart disease, phaeochromocytoma, depression, prostate or breast cancer history, a minoxidil allergy, choosing drops over capsules and declining finasteride, leads to exactly the same screens and the same bag: 'Prescription · Personalised treatment · 4 week supply · 12ml', £34.99. The real engine is a pharmacist prescriber who, after account creation and payment, picks one of 16 compounded formulas (6 capsules, 10 drops). Its published limits are the leaflet contraindications: no finasteride or dutasteride for women; no oral minoxidil with heart disease, phaeochromocytoma or uncontrolled blood pressure; no finasteride or dutasteride with prostate, breast, sexual-function or mental-health history; no drops on an inflamed or infected scalp; only niacinamide drops in pregnancy or breastfeeding. The company says the choice 'isn't automated or AI': a clinician reads the medical history, hair-loss pattern, lifestyle and goals and selects 'the right active ingredients and concentrations'. Its articles call finasteride first-line and dutasteride second-line (more advanced loss, marked crown thinning, or a limited response to finasteride), and point women with PCOS towards once-a-day minoxidil drops. Which strength a patient starts on is not published, and no prescription was seen.
companies.verdict: For the part anyone can see, this report is trustworthy. Two fresh baselines and 19 more replays in stage 3 reproduced every visible rule that was re-tested: the only stop is age under 18, a few answers add or skip one screen or add a badge, the promo links lower the first price, and the bag is always the same unnamed £34.99 'Personalised treatment'. No claim was contradicted. The corrections were about labels: a few rules and one option said 'observed' for something no replay can see (a prescriber's decision, a product removal or switch), and these now say 'none', 'docs' or 'inferred'. The product catalogue matches the live leaflets. The weak part is the real decision, which a pharmacist prescriber makes after sign-up and payment: what is said about who gets which formula comes from the company's leaflets and articles and from reasoning, so treat it as likely, not proven.
topOpportunities: Show the plan before the account wall: the likely medicine, strength and format, why it was chosen from the answers, and what was ruled out. Hair + Me shows one generic line to everyone, so a visible, explained recommendation is an immediate point of difference.

React to answers on screen. When someone ticks heart disease, uncontrolled blood pressure, a scalp infection or a minoxidil allergy, say at once what that means ('tablets are not suitable for you; here is what is') instead of staying silent until after payment.

Do real triage and be proud of it: route patchy, scarring-type or sudden loss to photos, a clinician call or a GP letter before any payment, and tell people with no hair loss that they do not need a prescription.

companies.accountWall: Hair and beard flows: after the last consent screen (finasteride statement in the hair flow). The next screen is an account form (first name, last name, email, phone, date of birth, password) titled "Based on your questionnaire results, we are now preparing your personalised health plan. companies.coverageNote: Stage 1 walked the baseline man to the account form and saw every conditional screen. Stage 2 replayed both baselines and then 45 one-change experiments live, each ending on the account form, the female stop notice or the sign-in page. Because no plan is shown before the account form, product effects could not be seen live: instead both copies of the recommendation code that the site serves to every visitor were run offline on the same one-change answers (28 further offline-only cases, plus all 32,768 combinations of the answers the code reads). Stage 3 (24 Nov 2026) replayed the baselines and the stop rules again (20 live replays in all), walked the partner-clinic route to its account form, confirmed that the survey definition and both copies of the recommendation code are unchanged, re-ran the newer code offline, and checked 14 live product pages and the product sitemap. companies.engineSummary: Sons runs one short questionnaire for men only. Sex at birth is the only gate: a woman is stopped at question 2, and a man is never stopped or warned, whatever he answers (33 live one-change replays all ended on the same account form). Nothing is recommended until he has given his name, email, phone number, date of birth and a password. After that a script in his own browser turns the answers into five on/off switches: finasteride tablet, finasteride spray, minoxidil capsule, minoxidil spray, combination spray. Each medical tick or reported side effect switches off a whole drug family: finasteride goes with a low-mood score of 2 or more, past finasteride side effects, kidney or liver disease, prostate disease or male cancers, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus or methotrexate, and sexual dysfunction; minoxidil (spray and capsule) goes with high blood pressure, heart disease and past minoxidil side effects; a scalp disorder removes the sprays that contain minoxidil; phaeochromocytoma removes the capsule; a lactose allergy removes both oral products; sudden onset removes everything on prescription. A fixed list of twelve plans is then filtered by the switches and the top one or two survivors are shown as "the plan our medical team recommend". The format preference only changes the order. The hair picture, the three sudden-onset follow-ups, the scalp tick boxes and all free text change nothing in this code. Strength never varies: each medicine comes in one strength. Hair Growth Complex, a supplement, is never removed, so there is always something to buy. Two copies of the code are served and they agree on everything except what goes first and what a man over 65 is shown. A prescriber at the partner pharmacy reviews the order afterwards and can refuse it; the server can also override the list. Those two steps are not public. Partner transplant-clinic pages work differently: they ask only the treatment type and procedure date, offer a free post-op pack when the procedure is within the next two months, and ask for an account before any medical question (seen live in stage 3).
companies.verdict: The questionnaire side of this report is trustworthy. Every stop, branch and extra screen that matters was replayed live at least once, the baselines replay identically a day later, and the survey definition is unchanged. The product side is trustworthy as code, not as observed fact: the rules that remove a drug family (sudden onset, PHQ-2, side effects, heart and blood pressure, finasteride exclusions, scalp disorder, lactose, over 65) match both copies of the served code line for line, both copies are still served byte-for-byte unchanged, and an independent offline re-run gives the stated plans. But no recommendation was seen live, the server can override the browser, and the prescriber's decisions are unknown, so these rules show what the site is built to offer, not what a patient finally receives. Stage 3 found no contradicted product rule. It corrected proof that pointed at a missing run folder, unlabelled 'observed' claims, an inaccurate 'silent' dead end in the beard flow, a beard warning that turned out to have no effect, and an untested partner-clinic route that asks for an account before any medical question. Prices and actives checked against 14 live product pages all matched.
topOpportunities: Show a provisional plan and price before asking for contact details. Sons shows nothing until an account exists.
Make the pattern and onset questions count: stop and refer patchy, sudden, scarring or infected-scalp cases with a clear explanation. Sons lets all of them through.
Tell the patient why a treatment is not offered and what the alternative is, instead of silently hiding plans.

companies.engineSummary: Numan's engine is simple. The server serves one question at a time and a few answers stop the consultation (under 18, patchy or complete loss, sudden onset, 65+ saying No), but every stop has a 'Review your answers' button that lets the patient change the answer and carry on. After each answer the server works out two yes/no flags, finasteride allowed and minoxidil allowed, plus an allergy list. The product screen hides every product containing a drug that is not allowed and features one product: the three-part kit by default, the product in the entry link if there was one (even when its drug is ruled out), or the first product left (Finasteride or Extra Strength Spray). Live tests show only seven answers move a flag: either drug allergy, scalp pain/itching, red rinds/rashes, any blood-pressure diagnosis (minoxidil off), and 'minoxidil only', specialist-managed mental health or recent suicidal thoughts (finasteride off). Everything else, including psoriasis/eczema and the patient's own 'I do not wish to be considered' answers for prostate monitoring, asthma and trying for a baby, changes nothing on screen: it only becomes a note for the clinician who reviews the order after payment details are taken. Pattern, age over 65 and preferences never change the offer. There is no dose or strength choice in the quiz: each product has one strength.
companies.verdict: Trustworthy as labelled. Every high-consequence rule I re-tested (ten of them, plus both baselines) gave exactly the recorded result, and the live catalogue and product pages match the recorded names, strengths and prices. I found no contradicted rule. The errors I found were small: two stops and one pair rule rested on code or a mixed walk (now observed), one opportunity wrongly said Numan has no topical finasteride, and one clinical opinion was not labelled. The new finding is that product entry links beat the eligibility flags as well as the allergy flags. The main limit is structural: the engine's flags are computed on Numan's server and everything after the account wall, including the clinician's final decision, is unseen, so the report describes what the anonymous quiz offers, not what is finally prescribed.
topOpportunities: Serve women: a female pattern hair-loss consultation (topical and oral minoxidil, spironolactone pathways) is entirely missing at Numan.
Honour patient choices at once: if someone opts out of a drug or a form, show only what they asked for, and explain why.

Offer strength and form choices (oral minoxidil, several minoxidil strengths, topical finasteride on its own). Numan has topical finasteride only inside its combination spray, and its quiz never asks about strength or form.

companies.engineSummary: Treated runs one short men-only questionnaire (11 questions, height and weight, a general medical profile) and then always shows the same five products with prices, with Finasteride 1mg pre-selected (or the product of the page the man came from). The answers do not choose the medicine. They decide two things: whether the man is stopped (female, or any history of mental illness), and whether the case is an automatic offer or goes to clinician review. That decision sits in the server response (mode Auto or Offline); the patient sees the same screen either way. Almost any non-standard answer, and simply never having used treatment or not having seen a doctor, sends the case to review, so most first-time buyers are reviewed after paying. Only in the automatic offer are per-product limits applied: smoking or any alcohol removes the two dutasteride products. Date of birth is asked only after the account wall. BMI over 35 sends the whole case to review, even from the Dutasteride link.
companies.verdict: Trustworthy as labelled for what an anonymous man sees. Both baselines and the eight highest-impact rules (female stop, mental-illness stop, smoking and alcohol removing dutasteride, product-link fallback, BMI, low blood pressure, review flags) were re-tested live and held. companies.engineSummary: Ro runs two different engines, and both can be read in full from code the site serves to any visitor. MEN: a 'soft steer' engine. Three marketing questions, then an email wall, then the medical questionnaire (the baseline man passes 19 screens up to the recommendation; reporting past treatments or conditions adds follow-ups). Nothing medical stops a man (only age under 18, female sex or an unserved zip code). Answers switch on up to three 'do not recommend' flags, one per treatment. A fixed priority list (Ro Mane Spray, then finasteride 1 mg tablets, then oral minoxidil 2.5 mg tablets) makes the first unflagged treatment the 'recommended' one, but all three stay on the screen and can be picked, on a default quarterly plan, and a clinician decides afterwards. In the offline one-change sweep the compounded spray, the dearest product, was recommended for every profile except: finasteride-type worries (depression, anxiety, erectile dysfunction, trying for a baby, past finasteride problems) which move the pick to oral minoxidil; prostate cancer or a topical allergy, which move it to finasteride tablets; and five 'another diagnosis?' answers (patches, very sudden onset, scalp redness, past steroid injections, persistently low blood pressure) which remove the recommendation but not the products. Heart and blood-pressure red flags only flag the minoxidil tablet, so the minoxidil spray stays recommended. Goals, severity and pattern only personalise a recap screen. WOMEN: a 'gate' engine. Three or four hair questions, then the sign-up wall, then the medical questionnaire (the baseline woman passes 31 screens up to the product choice). Pregnancy, any diagnosed scalp condition, signs of virilisation, lupus or autoimmune disease, past scalp steroid injections and minoxidil allergy end the visit with a referral. Breastfeeding, cardiovascular conditions, high blood pressure and age 66+ remove the tablet and leave only the compounded topical. Everyone else chooses between oral minoxidil ($30 a month) and Hair Solution Rx ($40 a month), with 'No preference' defaulting to the tablet; pattern, severity and symptoms never change the options. Before either wall the answers change only the wording or number of the next question (observed live); no product or price appears. Non-prescription products (5% minoxidil solution, shampoo, conditioner) are sold through separate links with no questions.
companies.verdict: Trustworthy as labelled. The pre-wall part (3 to 4 questions per flow) is fully observed: every option has now been replayed live and all 18 stage 3 replays matched what stage 2 recorded. The post-wall engine is not observed but is unusually well grounded: the consultation app downloads its complete question schema and the men's recommender in public code, both unchanged since stage 1, and an independent re-read of the raw schema and the current bundles agrees with every high-impact rule (women's hard stops, tablet removal for breastfeeding, heart and blood-pressure conditions and age 66+, the men's finasteride-to-oral-minoxidil switch, the spray > finasteride > oral minoxidil order). Treat post-wall rules as what the software is set to do before a clinician reviews the case, not as proof of what is finally prescribed; server-side state and clinician steps remain unknown.

Heart failure, heart attack, low blood pressure, pheochromocytoma, kidney disease, an allergy to minoxidil, earlier oral minoxidil, patchy, diffuse or sudden hair loss, a sore scalp, low mood, sexual dysfunction and age 61+ were each tried on their own, then together: same screens, same wording, same $65 cart, no warning. companies.verdict: For the one form that can be walked anonymously (oral minoxidil), this report is solid: the baseline replayed identically, every consequential rule re-tested live behaved exactly as recorded (two stops, the dose price, the free-text follow-up, and the "no effect" of heart failure and minoxidil allergy), the safety stop cannot be bypassed, and six new gap tests (including a woman) found nothing new. Product names, strengths and prices match the live pages, and the page-versus-form inconsistencies the report flags are real. The conclusion that the forms themselves make no clinical decision is well supported. The weaker parts are labelled honestly: the three walled forms and all old-checkout products (including the women's formula) are known from served code or marketing text only, and nothing about how the provider decides after checkout can be seen. Trust the "observed" and "code" items; treat the "docs" items about provider decisions as Strut's claims, not tested behaviour.

Make safety visible in the form: clear stop or warning screens for heart disease, low blood pressure and pregnancy, and "this may not be pattern hair loss, see a clinician" for patchy or sudden loss. Strut leaves all of this to an unseen review.
